title: Collector handshake compatibility layer and fanout shim for multi-backend exports
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: We operate a single ingest front door that must export spans to multiple downstream backends (Tempo, legacy Jaeger, and 3rd-party vendor sinks). Different backends expect slightly different OTLP variants, envelope formats, and metadata (deprecated attribute names, traceid/parentid length expectations, and sampling flag encodings). When downstreams change schema or go through rolling upgrades the current export path has caused dropped spans, schema mismatches, and manual operator intervention. We also lack a robust per-tenant priority fanout that supports connection pooling and graceful backpressure signaling to avoid head-of-line blocking when one backend is slow.

Objective: Implement a collector-side compatibility/handshake layer plus a fanout shim that:
- Negotiates exporter protocol semantics at connection start (detect proto version, supported compression, and mTLS requirements).
- Performs targeted span transformations (attribute name remapping, optional truncation rules for incompatible backends, and legacy-jaeger envelope wrapping when required).
- Exposes a per-tenant fanout policy engine (priority lanes: realtime, standard, archival) and connection pool per backend to limit concurrent gRPC streams.
- Implements backpressure-aware retries/backoff by mapping gRPC status codes and exporter health signals to per-tenant write window throttles.
- Ships with feature-flag gating and canary rollout plan, plus end-to-end integration tests against Tempo and Jaeger-in-memory test clusters.

Design notes & trade-offs:
- Transformation vs. canonicalization: We avoid permanent canonicalization (mutating canonical traceid) to preserve fidelity for debugging; instead apply non-destructive mapping rules and attach a metadata marker on transformed spans for trace rehydration tools.
- CPU/memory overhead: Prototype showed ~2.8% additional CPU per-1000 spans when running attribute mapping and envelope wrapping. We measured a 6-8% increase in p95 export latency under a synthetic topology with three downstreams. We will mitigate by only enabling heavy transforms for tenants that require legacy compatibility (per-tenant opt-in to avoid cluster-wide overhead).
- Connection pooling: Using a bounded pool per-backend reduces connection churn but adds queueing latency for bursts. Policy tuning will be surfaced in Console as per-tenant knobs (pool_size, max_queue_ms).
- Security: mTLS requirement negotiation occurs during handshake; the shim supports credential rotation using our existing credential-rotation service. No plaintext fallback permitted for tenants with encryption_required flag.

Implementation plan:
1) Spike and prototype (done) - small Go collector module that accepts OTLP spans, runs transformation pipeline, and dispatches to backend clients with pooled gRPC channels.
2) Tests: unit tests for transformer rules, integration tests against tempo-dev and jaeger-dev clusters, and chaos tests simulating exporter slowdowns (sigterm, hung streams).
3) Feature flag & config: implement gate in Config Service (feature: "collector.fanout_compat_v1") and per-tenant policy stored in tenant-configs.
4) Metrics & dashboards: emit exporter.handshake.success, exporter.handshake.failure_reason, exporter.queue_length_by_backend, exporter.pool_utilization, and exporter.transformation_count. Add latency/error dashboards and an alert when exporter.fail_rate > 0.5% for 5m on customer-facing tiers.
5) Rollout: Canary in region us-west-2 for low-usage tenants -> expand to internal tenants -> open beta for opt-in external customers -> gradual ramp.

Acceptance criteria:
- All integration tests pass in CI against tempo-dev + jaeger-dev.
- Metric coverage present and dashboards created in Console (links below).
- Canary stable for 48h with fail_rate < 0.1% and no increase in tail downstream latencies beyond agreed SLOs.
- Documentation: Confluence design doc and runbook completed.

Artifacts & links:
- Design doc: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1fExampleDesignDoc
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/observability/pull/1872
- Integration test harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/trace-tests/tree/main/collector-fanout
- Console dashboard draft: https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/exporter-fanout-compat

Risks & mitigations:
- Risk: Silent data loss if transformation has an unknown edge-case. Mitigation: Transformer runs in dry-run mode initially (adds a marker and logs a sample of transformations instead of mutating), escalate to full mode after signoff.
- Risk: Backpressure amplification causing whole-collector slowdown. Mitigation: implement per-backend leaky-bucket and global shedder with SLO-aware thresholds.

Next steps (short-term):
- Address PR feedback (security/line-by-line comments from infra-reviewers), specifically around credential handling and credential rotation during rehandshake (PR 1872 comment thread).
- Add e2e latency SLO test in CI that simulates 10k spans/s with one slow backend to validate pooled connections and queue thresholds.
- Prepare runbook and alerting for canary.

Estimated timeline: 2 sprints to delivery (prototype + tests + canary) assuming no blocking infra work.
